author: Kevin Carson
title: A Half-Built Garden, by Ruthanna Emrys (Tor 2022)
content:
A Half-Built Garden is a well thought out first contact story, with an engaging plot — things which would make it well worth reading on its own. But as anyone familiar with my previous reviews will be aware, when I review near-future sci-fi stories about liberatory postcapitalist utopias, that’s not my primary concern. I review them for their future history worldbuilding — a sin comparable to Auden’s reading the Bible for its prose.

The story is set in the 2080s, following a mid-century Time of Troubles, when the world is emerging from the ruins of capitalism and creating a new, humanly tolerable society.

The dominant governing institution is the watershed network, a federation of self-managed local institutions more or less equivalent to bioregions, which incorporates most of the world’s population and resources. The balance of power is the result of a mostly non-violent mid-century revolution beginning a generation or two earlier, in which a combination of boycotts, sabotage, and other direct action forced the corporations into offshore enclaves. The viewpoint character, who inhabits the Chesapeake Watershed, reminisces about the days when her parents “helped place the first illicit sensors in the Potomac and barricaded factories to enforce the first crowdsourced decisions of the nascent Dandelion Revolution.”

The corporations, as is typical for this genre, consist of “billionaire lords and serf-employees huddled behind their fencelines on their artificial islands.” Their inhabitants, aside from “a few converts and visitors,” are “only the descendants of the people who’d arrived with their founder — allies and employees who’d prioritized fleeing apocalypse over creating community to stop it.”

Corporate enclaves were bounded by “fencelines,” apparently imposed from outside by the networks during the course of the Dandelion Revolution. “As for the corporations, eventually we didn’t allow it. People like my parents organized to stop them, and created the first watershed networks.” Actions taken during the Revolution ranged from “setting limits on their carbon production to get warming under control, to blocking their shipping if they went over their carbon budgets.” The corporations, “which couldn’t bear the transformation, …eventually… barricaded themselves behind their own fencelines on a few artificial islands….”

The corporations, since their relegation to island enclaves, have mostly refused any official recognition of the watersheds’ existence, and for their own part “lost any legal existence outside their own territory a long time ago.” They send observers to carbon talks, tacitly obey the carbon and other pollutant budgets the watersheds, as dominant actors, lay down for them, and cheat when they think they can evade detection. Their relative lack of power means they must file impact reports for approval by neighboring regional watershed consortia in cases where projects might have an impact beyond the fencelines.

Most of the corporations’ former economic functions, aside from a dwindling number of areas in which they still possess a monopoly on the necessary technical expertise, have been taken over by the watersheds. Some pre-watershed industrial resources have been absorbed by the watersheds — e.g. “MIT and the Pan-Asian Maker Collective” are “hooked into the dandelion networks.”

Overall, relations between watersheds and corporations amount to a cold war.

“We still buy from them, sometimes….. Things we need that we haven’t been able to back-engineer yet, or exchanges that someone thinks will eventually incentivize them to join us. And they’re allowed out among the watersheds as long as they promise to behave.”

The watersheds’ primary focus in dealing with the corporations is managing their decline — taking over their remaining indispensable functions, and in the meantime maintaining contact to encourage internal culture change and preventing any desperate rear-guard action that will get a lot of people killed.

“They’re not going to disappear any time soon — someone has to keep talking to them, or they’ll never change enough to join the rest of the world….

“We still need them. They almost broke the world, when they had power — but the corporations still make key parts of our network infrastructure. They think they need us because without those exports, they lose any justification for their continued existence. But really, that tenuous connection is their last chance to find a new justification. Every time we interact, it reminds them that there’s another way. Every freelance contract keeps the window open. When we finally take over the last of the manufacturing, the opportunity to change them vanishes — and we might need to fight the dandelion revolution all over again. I’d rather take them into the future with us.”

Nation-states still persist, but with significantly less power as the result both of the Dandelion Revolution and of their own fiscal and material exhaustion. Although most production, distribution, and governance is handled by the watersheds, nation-states still claim territorial sovereignty over the watersheds and their inhabitants (which themselves apparently comprise most of the earth’s land area). The mostly hollowed-out states (referred to at one point as “fossil states”) carry out a major share of their functions through the watersheds, with some minimal recognition of their sovereignty by the latter, in much the same way the later western Roman Empire did through German tribal authorities.

In response to a visiting extraterrestrial’s question “So how does the United States of America relate to the Chesapeake Bay Watershed Network,” a NASA representative replies, “Technically, this is U.S. territory. A national park.”

The watersheds function internally as a sort of digitally networked hybrid of direct democracy, consensus, and the sort of p2p ad hocracy depicted in Cory Doctorow’s Down and Out in the Magic Kingdom and Walkaway .

The dandelion communications network was designed from the ground up during the mid-century Blackouts, with an architecture aimed at facilitating such a communication style.

The dandelion networks had been created in the wake of massive malware and malinformation epidemics, first as a way to maintain communications while preserving data, then as a way to reshape and reclaim those data as tools for justice and survival.

To take one example, the Chesapeake Watershed Network put together a contact team for the alien spacecraft in their territory by putting out calls for people with previous negotiating experience with other networks, and with corporations or states, as well as biologists, and then up- or down-voting the selectees.

More generally, policy and governance questions are addressed in a stigmergic or wikified way by members posting problems or proposed solutions to the network, followed by an open-ended process of debate and up- and down-voting. Network “weighting and aggregation algorithms” coordinated decisionmaking by “threading, …constantly picking out key ideas and sorting possible approaches and marking the valence and weight of our responses.”

The interaction between the dandelion communication platform, individual members, and local economies is reminiscent of the Acquis in Bruce Sterling’s The Caryatids and D-Space in Daniel Suarez’s Freedom( ) . As the viewpoint character describes her interface with the network:

Then I got up and retrieved my mesh from its stand, settled the cool smartmail back over my bare scalp, and let the Network flow back into my lenses….

I eased in, catching up on half-deserted policy decisions. Streambed restoration for the Paint Branch, a proposal for using a new algae species in water treatment, the carbon budget for importing tea and coffee. There were still a few people working on those threads, refining options and adding weight to their favorites.

As I said, I review science fiction primarily for the future history timelines and other worldbuilding, rather than for the plot. But the latter is also quite engaging. Like Emrys’ Innsmouth reboots, this story wraps up — spoiler alert — with a satisfying inter-species entente.

If you’re a fan of fiction set in a better world the day after tomorrow, as an escape or source of inspiration in the face of an increasingly scary tomorrow, I highly recommend this book. In many ways it reminds me of both the utopian alternative in Marge Piercy’s Woman On the Edge of Time , and the Walkaway society in Cory Doctorow’s novel of the same name, and has earned itself a space beside them as one of my favorites of the genre.

author: Alexandra Bradbury
title: Letter Carriers Set to Deliver Change in Upcoming Union Election
content:
A leadership change looks likely in the Letter Carriers (NALC) this fall. Members are mad about low pay and forced overtime, dangerous heat and robberies, the rejected contract imposed last year, the backlog of tens of thousands of grievances, and the president’s secretive approach to bargaining.

There’s not just one group pushing for change, but a whole ecosystem of reform groups, slates, and podcasters among the 5,000-plus delegates coming to Los Angeles for the union convention August 3-7. They’ll rub elbows and hopefully build unity at a “ Reformers Rum Party ” on Sunday night, the eve of the convention.

Days before the August 5 nominations, it looks like a three-way race for president. The 200,000 members will get the chance to vote this fall—by mail ballot, of course—for 10 officers, three trustees, and 15 regional business agents.

Two reform tickets have been campaigning for two years. One is the Concerned Letter Carriers (CLC) slate, headlined by current Vice President James Henry and including a number of branch (local) presidents. The other is Mike Caref , business agent for Illinois, running solo for president.

Despite months of speculation about whether President Brian Renfroe would run again, he still hasn’t made any announcment. But a third slate announced July 17 includes many other incumbents, led by Eddie Davidson, current business agent for Florida, Georgia, and the Carolinas.

DOOMSDAY CLOCK

The backdrop is ongoing existential threats to USPS. Since Trump returned to office, the postal doomsday clock has been minutes from midnight .

Though Trump hasn’t acted on his threat to move the Postal Service under the Department of Commerce, his new batch of nominees for the Board of Governors aren’t even from private sector logistics, but from finance—so maybe less interested in rationalizing the service than in selling it for parts.

Postmaster General David Steiner, who somehow makes his predecessor Louis DeJoy look good, is going along with Trump’s extreme attacks on vote by mail. He says USPS won’t deliver ballots in states that won’t hand over voter lists to the government.

Steiner has also been claiming USPS could run out of money within the year, and threatening to close post offices and cut delivery days if its finances aren’t fixed.

The next-biggest union, the Postal Workers (APWU), organized rallies July 28 for three reforms that would help in the short term—raise the debt limit, modify the investment strategy for retiree benefit funds (they’re all in treasury bonds), and change how the retirement obligation is calculated.

Longer-term, USPS needs to adapt to fewer letters and more packages. Management’s approach has been to cut costs by degrading service. The unions argue it should instead expand revenue by adding services like banking, Internet access, hunting licenses, electric vehicle charging, and checking in on seniors.

In addition, retired letter carrier and longtime activist Jamie Partridge argues, the government should subsidize rural delivery, as many other countries do.

OVERLAPPING GROUPS

A vote-no movement on the 2024 contract was organized by a coalition of forces including Caref, the CLC, the Build a Fighting NALC (BFN) caucus, and influential podcaster Corey Walton, number two on the CLC ticket.

Podcasts are big with letter carriers—you can listen while you slog through the workday. One called “Next Generation Carriers” has interviewed activists from all the vying groups and even Renfroe himself ( Labor Notes staffers have also been guests). Co-host Margo O’Neill, a steward of Branch 352 in Des Moines, is also the treasurer for BFN. Her main goals at the convention, she said, are to grow the reach of the reform movement and to build unity across the various existing groups.

The Next Gen hosts have been agitating for a contract demand of “30 for 30”: a starting wage of $30 and no more than one manager per 30 carriers, to save money and alleviate micromanagement. New carriers start at about $21 , in an entry-level job called “city carrier assistant” where they’re often made to work Sundays delivering Amazon packages. It can take two years to convert to a career position, and even then, everyone hired since 2013 is on second-tier Table 2 pay.

In the Massachusetts chapter of BFN, “we’ve been really pushing to get people more active, talking to CCAs about their rights on the job,” said Chris Persampieri, legislative and political director of Branch 18. “A lot of people had no idea that if it’s your day off, you’re not on call. You don’t have to pick up the phone.

“There’s no union steward on Amazon Sundays, so they’re on their own. We show up with flyers about their rights and a box of joe from Dunkin’ Donuts, because it’s Massachusetts and that’s what we do here.”

Some reform activists are backing the CLC; some are backing Caref; some like certain members of the Davidson slate. The election may yield a mixed executive council of people who ran on opposing tickets, and the new president will have to “mold that into a solid team,” said Branch 3 President David Grosskopf of Buffalo, who’s running for trustee with the CLC.

CONTRACT DEBACLE

What's difficult to find is anyone with a good word to say about Renfroe. Last convention he was already in hot water, facing internal charges of dereliction of duty and impaired driving of a union vehicle.

Delegates voted to let him off the hook. But they also voted for more member involvement and substantive bargaining updates; Renfroe had been bargaining for nearly two years in near-complete secrecy.

Soon afterward, he came out with a tentative agreement featuring a measly 1.3 percent annual raise. Members voted it down.

As the union returned to the table in early 2025, Renfroe announced nationwide “Fight Like Hell” rallies—then reversed course over fears of Trump and DOGE, and rushed into binding arbitration. The arbitrator imposed a contract nearly identical to the one members had voted down, sparking more outrage.

And the bad deal had taken so long to negotiate that it was more than half over, expiring in May 2026, so NALC was soon back at the table.

The union has made incremental improvements in its approach this time. There was a member survey, a national day of rallies, some video updates, and a collective bargaining conference for branch and state leaders.

Still, as the 60-day mediation period expired in July, meaning the union could be moving to arbitration, members had little information. “We have no idea what economic package our union is asking for,” Grosskopf said. “We don’t know if we’re asking for $30 an hour, or $50.”

Renfroe has kept even fellow officers at arm’s length from bargaining. The last straw for Mack Julion, assistant secretary-treasurer, was when the president proposed a four-day workweek of 10-hour days, meaning carriers would no longer get overtime pay after eight hours.

“Ours is a physically demanding job,” Julion said. “I’m kinda known for my fancy cowboy boots; I wear those because I have a bad case of plantar fasciitis. I’ve known many letter carriers who had hip replacements and knee surgeries.

“I had suggested hazard pay,” he said. “If you think a four by 10 schedule is a higher priority than hazard pay when we’re just a couple years removed from Covid, and we have letter carriers literally dying in the heat ... We are human, and we break down.”

Rather than run again with Renfroe, Julion planned to run independently for reelection. He ended up joining the Davidson slate.

DEMOCRACY IN ACTION

The convention has strongly democratic features. There are no major hurdles to getting nominated. Delegates vote on every constitutional amendment or resolution submitted by any branch or state association—this year there are many.

Persampieri authored an amendment for ranked-choice voting (where voters can indicate their second- and third-choice candidates and the resulting votes are tabulated in “instant runoffs”), to remove the fear of voting for a spoiler. Branch 3 proposed that the national bargaining team include five officers, not just the president.

Delegates may hear internal charges brought against the officers by a San Diego carrier, Michael Rivera, over the imposition of the rejected contract last year. The officers declined to investigate the charges against themselves, but Rivera is appealing to the convention body.

They will also elect delegates to the 2030 AFL-CIO convention. A “Stand-Up Slate” of younger carriers is running on themes like universal health care and the abolition of billionaires.

Some resolutions were submitted calling on the union to livestream the convention, which officers decided to do.

Minneapolis Branch 9 has sent resolutions on political themes, like ending the war in Iran and funding public services. BFN activist Tyler Vasseur warned first-time delegates not to be too disappointed if they don’t pass.

“The idea is to force a debate on the issue,” he said. “If we get 20 to 30 percent of the vote, we can identify people who want to fight and get organized on these issues going forward.”

WINS NEEDED

Getting members into motion is the name of the game. “If we’re ever going to get the participation up in the union, people have to feel there’s a fight going on, and we have to get some wins,” Caref said. “We’ve been taking a lot of losses, and it’s really demoralizing for the carriers.

“You've got to start with a clear vision for where you want to be, and a strategy for how you’re gonna get there. You get some little wins, you get more people involved, and you start moving in the right direction.

“That’s why I always tell people, I only want to be president if you guys want me to be president,” he said, “because I’m going to give you stuff to do right away.”

Correction: This article originally misstated the expiration date of the last contract. It has been expired since May 22, 2026.

Postmaster General David Steiner, who somehow makes his predecessor Louis DeJoy look good, is going along with Trump’s extreme attacks on vote by mail. He says USPS won’t deliver ballots in states that won’t hand over voter lists to the government.
Steiner has also been claiming USPS could run out of money within the year, and threatening to close post offices and cut delivery days if its finances aren’t fixed.

The next-biggest union, the Postal Workers (APWU), organized rallies July 28 for three reforms that would help in the short term—raise the debt limit, modify the investment strategy for retiree benefit funds (they’re all in treasury bonds), and change how the retirement obligation is calculated.

Longer-term, USPS needs to adapt to fewer letters and more packages. Management’s approach has been to cut costs by degrading service. The unions argue it should instead expand revenue by adding services like banking, Internet access, hunting licenses, electric vehicle charging, and checking in on seniors.
In addition, retired letter carrier and longtime activist Jamie Partridge argues, the government should subsidize rural delivery, as many other countries do.
OVERLAPPING GROUPS

A vote-no movement on the 2024 contract was organized by a coalition of forces including Caref, the CLC, the Build a Fighting NALC (BFN) caucus, and influential podcaster Corey Walton, number two on the CLC ticket.

Podcasts are big with letter carriers—you can listen while you slog through the workday. One called “Next Generation Carriers” has interviewed activists from all the vying groups and even Renfroe himself ( Labor Notes staffers have also been guests). Co-host Margo O’Neill, a steward of Branch 352 in Des Moines, is also the treasurer for BFN. Her main goals at the convention, she said, are to grow the reach of the reform movement and to build unity across the various existing groups.

The Next Gen hosts have been agitating for a contract demand of “30 for 30”: a starting wage of $30 and no more than one manager per 30 carriers, to save money and alleviate micromanagement. New carriers start at about $21 , in an entry-level job called “city carrier assistant” where they’re often made to work Sundays delivering Amazon packages. It can take two years to convert to a career position, and even then, everyone hired since 2013 is on second-tier Table 2 pay.

In the Massachusetts chapter of BFN, “we’ve been really pushing to get people more active, talking to CCAs about their rights on the job,” said Chris Persampieri, legislative and political director of Branch 18. “A lot of people had no idea that if it’s your day off, you’re not on call. You don’t have to pick up the phone.

“There’s no union steward on Amazon Sundays, so they’re on their own. We show up with flyers about their rights and a box of joe from Dunkin’ Donuts, because it’s Massachusetts and that’s what we do here.”

Some reform activists are backing the CLC; some are backing Caref; some like certain members of the Davidson slate. The election may yield a mixed executive council of people who ran on opposing tickets, and the new president will have to “mold that into a solid team,” said Branch 3 President David Grosskopf of Buffalo, who’s running for trustee with the CLC.
CONTRACT DEBACLE

What's difficult to find is anyone with a good word to say about Renfroe. Last convention he was already in hot water, facing internal charges of dereliction of duty and impaired driving of a union vehicle.
Delegates voted to let him off the hook. But they also voted for more member involvement and substantive bargaining updates; Renfroe had been bargaining for nearly two years in near-complete secrecy.
Soon afterward, he came out with a tentative agreement featuring a measly 1.3 percent annual raise. Members voted it down.

As the union returned to the table in early 2025, Renfroe announced nationwide “Fight Like Hell” rallies—then reversed course over fears of Trump and DOGE, and rushed into binding arbitration. The arbitrator imposed a contract nearly identical to the one members had voted down, sparking more outrage.
And the bad deal had taken so long to negotiate that it was more than half over, expiring in May 2026, so NALC was soon back at the table.

The union has made incremental improvements in its approach this time. There was a member survey, a national day of rallies, some video updates, and a collective bargaining conference for branch and state leaders.

Still, as the 60-day mediation period expired in July, meaning the union could be moving to arbitration, members had little information. “We have no idea what economic package our union is asking for,” Grosskopf said. “We don’t know if we’re asking for $30 an hour, or $50.”

Renfroe has kept even fellow officers at arm’s length from bargaining. The last straw for Mack Julion, assistant secretary-treasurer, was when the president proposed a four-day workweek of 10-hour days, meaning carriers would no longer get overtime pay after eight hours.

“Ours is a physically demanding job,” Julion said. “I’m kinda known for my fancy cowboy boots; I wear those because I have a bad case of plantar fasciitis. I’ve known many letter carriers who had hip replacements and knee surgeries.

“I had suggested hazard pay,” he said. “If you think a four by 10 schedule is a higher priority than hazard pay when we’re just a couple years removed from Covid, and we have letter carriers literally dying in the heat ... We are human, and we break down.”
Rather than run again with Renfroe, Julion planned to run independently for reelection. He ended up joining the Davidson slate.
DEMOCRACY IN ACTION

The convention has strongly democratic features. There are no major hurdles to getting nominated. Delegates vote on every constitutional amendment or resolution submitted by any branch or state association—this year there are many.

Persampieri authored an amendment for ranked-choice voting (where voters can indicate their second- and third-choice candidates and the resulting votes are tabulated in “instant runoffs”), to remove the fear of voting for a spoiler. Branch 3 proposed that the national bargaining team include five officers, not just the president.

Delegates may hear internal charges brought against the officers by a San Diego carrier, Michael Rivera, over the imposition of the rejected contract last year. The officers declined to investigate the charges against themselves, but Rivera is appealing to the convention body.
They will also elect delegates to the 2030 AFL-CIO convention. A “Stand-Up Slate” of younger carriers is running on themes like universal health care and the abolition of billionaires.
Some resolutions were submitted calling on the union to livestream the convention, which officers decided to do.

Minneapolis Branch 9 has sent resolutions on political themes, like ending the war in Iran and funding public services. BFN activist Tyler Vasseur warned first-time delegates not to be too disappointed if they don’t pass.
“The idea is to force a debate on the issue,” he said. “If we get 20 to 30 percent of the vote, we can identify people who want to fight and get organized on these issues going forward.”
WINS NEEDED

Getting members into motion is the name of the game. “If we’re ever going to get the participation up in the union, people have to feel there’s a fight going on, and we have to get some wins,” Caref said. “We’ve been taking a lot of losses, and it’s really demoralizing for the carriers.

“You've got to start with a clear vision for where you want to be, and a strategy for how you’re gonna get there. You get some little wins, you get more people involved, and you start moving in the right direction.
“That’s why I always tell people, I only want to be president if you guys want me to be president,” he said, “because I’m going to give you stuff to do right away.”

title: Freispruch wegen Adbustings gegen Bundeswehr-Naziprepper
content:
Soldaten der Bundeswehr als „Nazi-Prepper“ zu bezeichnen? „Ist ok!“ entschied das Amtsgericht Schwerin. Denn die Meinungsfreiheit gelte auch für Adbustings, die die Bundeswehr kritisieren. Die Staatsanwaltschaft zieht nun ihre zuvor eingereichte Berufung zurück. Kai  N. Krieger vom Antimilitaristischen Aktionsnetzwerk (a2n) freut sich: „Zu Recht endet diese Farce eines  Prozesses mit einer Schlappe für die Staatsanwaltschaft. Dieser Kriminalisierungsversuch war skandalös. Ab jetzt sollte sich der Staatsapparat um die Nazi-Prepper kümmern, anstatt diejenigen zu verurteilen, die die Botschaft übermitteln.“

Beleidigung wegen Bundeswehr-Adbustings?

Das Amtsgericht Schwerin hat am Dienstag, den 10.03.2026 zwei Antimilitaristen freigesprochen. Daraufhin legte die Staatsanwaltschaft Berufung ein. Sie hatte den Aktivisten „Beleidigung aller aktiven Soldaten der Bundeswehr“ vorgeworfen. Jetzt hat die Staatsanwaltschaft die Berufung zurückgezogen. Der Freispruch ist damit rechtsgültig. Im Jahr zuvor kritisierten Antimilitarist*innen in Schwerin und in weiteren 15 deutschen Städten den zum ersten Mal stattfindenden Veteranentag. Dafür platzierten sie unerlaubt eigene Poster im Design der Bundeswehr in Werbevitrinen. Mit Sprüchen wie: „Abhängen mit Nazi-Preppern? Nein zum Veteranentag!“ und „Deutscher Mix: Nazis, Patronen, Einzelfälle“ machten sie auf das Nazi-Problem in der Bundeswehr aufmerksam.

https://antimil-aktionsnetzwerk.site36.net/2025/06/15/adbusting-protest-gegen-den-veteranentag-in-13-staedten/

Adbusting-Alarm im Naziprepper-Land

Schwerin: Das ist die Hauptstadt der Naziprepper vom Nordkreuz. Die Mitglieder der Terrorbande waren Polizisten, Militärs, Juristen und Politiker. Sie klauten Waffen und Munition bei ihren Arbeitgeber*innen, legten Todeslisten mit Namen und Adressen an, und bestellten bereits Löschkalk und Leichensäcke. Besonders brisant: Der Chef der Heimatschutzkompanie, die wenige Wochen später Liegenschaften beim G20-Gipfel in Hamburg unterstützen sollte, ist beteiligt. Er wollte den Nazi-Preppern für ihre geplanten Mordtaten Papiere und LKWs der Bundeswehr zur Verfügung stellen.

Ausgerechnet bei den Cops in Mecklenburg sorgte die Adbusting- Aktion für Großalarm. Begründung: „ Bundeswehrfeindliche Plakate“ Im Strafgesetzbuch gibt es keinen Paragrafen, der eine eventuelle „Bundeswehrfeindschaft“ verbietet . Die Polizeiinspektion Stralsund meint (https://www.presseportal.de/blaulicht/pm/108767/6054960) jedoch: „ (…)diese Art des kreativen Protestes ist keineswegs ein satirischer Witz, sondern kann vielmehr den Tatbestand von Ordnungswidrigkeiten oder auch Straftaten erfüllen.“ „Es wäre schön, wenn die Mecklenburger Cops ihre Nazi-Prepper-Kollegen, die Mitglied in der Nazi-Terror-Bande „Nordkreuz“ waren, so engagiert verfolgen und rausschmeißen würden.“  kommentiert dies Kai N. Krieger.

„Auch unbequemes Adbusting ist grundrechtlich geschützt“

Die Werbevitrinen im öffentlichen Raum lassen sich mit handelsüblichen Rohsteckschlüsseln aus dem Baumarkt öffnen. Daher scheiden Sachbeschädigung und Diebstahl bereits aus. Deswegen versuchte die Staatsanwaltschaft Schwerin, die Adbustings als „Beleidigung aller aktiven Soldaten“ zu übersehen. Was die Staatsanwaltschaft bei ihrer Verfolgung Unschuldiger übersah: Genau das ist erlaubt:  Das Bundesverfassungsgericht stellte u.a. im bekannten Urteil zu  „Soldaten sind Mörder!“ im Jahr 1995 klar, dass man so etwas sagen darf, ohne bestraft zu werden. Denn „alle Soldaten“ sei keine hinreichend zählbare Einschränkung, so dass sich eine konkrete Soldat*in beleidigt fühlen müsse. Auch Politik und Institutionen dürfen straffrei beleidigt werden.

„Auch unbequemes Adbusting ist grundrechtlich geschützt“ schreibt Prof. Dr. Fischer-Lescano in einem Gutachten dazu:

https://verfassungsblog.de/adbusting-unbequem-aber-grundrechtlich-geschuetzt/

Folgerichtig erklärte auch das Bundesverfassungsgericht aus Karlsruhe im Dezember 2023 eine Hausdurchsuchung der Berliner Polizei wegen Adbustings für illegal:

https://www.bundesverfassungsgericht.de/SharedDocs/Pressemitteilungen/DE/2023/bvg23-121.html

Erst im August 2025 stellte das Amtsgericht Tiergarten in Berlin ein Verfahren wegen Polizei-Adbustings ein:

https://antifawerkstatt.noblogs.org/post/2025/08/25/gewonnen-prozess-wegen-polizei-adbustings-endet-mit-einstellung/

Vor der Verhandlung hatten die Betroffenen ihrem Strafbefehl von einmal 20 Tagessätzen zu 20 Euro sowie 40 Tagessätze zu 40 Euro widersprochen. In den Gerichtssaal begleiteten die Angeklagten etwa ein Dutzend solidarische Menschen, zahlreiche Journalisten, und vier zivile Angehörige von LKA, Staatsschutz, Verfassungsschutz und Co. Einer davon trug ein T-Shirt mit einer Abbildung des bei Nazis als Symbol beliebten „Spartaner-Helm“.

Gleich mehrere Journalist:innen, solidarische Menschen und Zuschauerinnen wurden Zeugen von der Gewalt mit der Justizbeamte gegen Menschen vorgehen, die Wasser trinken oder eine laute solidarische Bemerkung machen. Beim Einlass in den Saal kam es zu strengen Kontrollen. Justizvollzugsbeamte durchsuchten die Taschen eines Journalisten und drohten ihm mit Rauswurf. Außerdem wurden sämtliche Smartphones und Ausweise der Zuschauenden beschlagnahmt.

Während der Verhandlung kam es zu Tumult im Zuschauer*Innenbereich. Der Schweriner Justizvollzugs-Beamte Sebastian Horn störte die Verhandlung massiv. Er brachte einen solidarischen Menschen mit Hilfe von roher Gewalt und Schmerzgriffen aus dem Saal. Herr Horn handelte dabei ohne Weisung des Richters und deshalb rechtswidrig. Kai N. Krieger findet: „ Wenn die Staatsanwaltschaft legitimen Protest statt Naziprepper verfolgt, dann verwundert auch der Rechtsbruch der Gerichtsbeamten keineswegs. „

Im Plädoyer nahm der Staatsanwalt indirekt Bezug auf die „Soldaten-sind-Mörder!“-Rechtsprechung. Er behauptete, dass die ca. 180.000 Angehörigen der Bundeswehr zählbar seien, und forderte eine Verurteilung. Davor redete er noch Unsinn von irgendwas mit Waffen-SS und so.

Doch der Richter entschied am Ende der gut besuchten Verhandlung auf Freispruch. Er hatte extra eine Präsentation mit den Adbustings vom Veteranentag vorbereitet. Er sagte, er könne gar nicht verurteilen, da er an höhere Rechtsprechung gebunden sei. Der Richter berief sich auf die Meinungsfreiheit §5 GG. Kritik gegenüber Institutionen sei demokratisch. Der Richter erklärte, dass die Forderung „Nein zum Veteranentag“ auf den Postern des Antimilitaristischen Aktionsnetzwerk ein Beitrag zur Sache und in diesem Fall die Meinungsfreiheit wichtiger sei als vermeintliche individuelle Betroffenheit von Nazipreppern. Die Bezeichnung von Soldat*innen als „Nazi-Prepper“ auf gefälschten Bundeswehrplakaten sei legal, solange sie in einem politischen Kontext stehe.

Die Presse berichtete ausführlich über den Freispruch https://antimil-aktionsnetzwerk.site36.net/2026/03/10/pressespiegel-adbusting-prozess-schwerin/

Die Staatsanwaltschaft akzeptierte das Urteil zuerst nicht und ging in Berufung. Jetzt zog sie die Berufung von sich aus zurück. Dadurch ist die Gerichtsentscheidung nun vollends rechtskräftigt. „Das Urteil bestätigt, was in einer Demokratie klar sein sollte: Nazi-Prepper darf man Nazi-Prepper nennen! Jetzt wo die Staatsanwaltschaft die eindeutige Entscheidung endlich doch akzeptiert hat, sollte sie nun die Nazi-Prepper vor Gericht bringen, der Anlass der Adbusting-Aktion waren.“ findet Kai N. Krieger.

Wie das alles zustande kam, könnt ihr in den Chroniken, welche Behörden sich alles über die Adbustings zum Veteranentag geärgert haben, nachlesen:

https://antimil-aktionsnetzwerk.site36.net/2025/10/29/verfolgung-von-militaerkritischen-adbusterinnen/

title: Zum Attentat auf den CSD von radikalen Queers: Kraft und Mut zur queeren kollektiven Selbstverteidigung!
content:
Kraft und Mut zur queeren kollektiven Selbstverteidigung!

Wir schreiben diesen Text mit wütenden, traurigen, zärtlichen und widerständigen Herzen.

Nach den erschütternden, aber bereits befürchteten Ereignissen am Christopher Street Day in Berlin (Samstag, 25. Juli), ist einmal mehr offensichlich, dass wir unseren Schutz und unsere Leben selber organisieren müssen.

Dies ist ein Aufruf zur kollektiven Selbstverteidigung und dazu, sich die Straße zurück zu nehmen, unabhängig davon, was die Polizei und der Staat dazu sagen. Denn unseren „Schutz gewährleisten“ können sie nie, auch wenn sie gerade mal nicht selber die anti-queere Gewalt ausüben.

Unsere Lebensweisen als queere, als migrantische, als trans, als behinderte Menschen und als Frauen werden immer wieder angegriffen durch gewalttätige patriarchale, autoritäre und faschistische Personen, Gruppierungen und Strukturen, wie z.B. auch die AfD. In diesem Sinne rufen wir dazu auf, uns zu organisieren und diesen Angriffen entschlossen, mit gegenseitiger Fürsorge und Solidarität und auch der notwendigen Militanz entgegenzutreten.

Wir stellen uns klar gegen die rassistische und anti-muslimische Instrumentalisierung der Tat.

Wir schicken allen Betroffenen, Trauernden und Kämpfenden Kraft und den Mut zum Widerstand.

Mehr queere Riots! Remember Stonewall!

Liebevolle und solidarische Grüße aus dem LesBiSchwulTransQueeren* Tortenessen, Bern

Courage for collective queer self defense!

Dies ist ein Aufruf zur kollektiven Selbstverteidigung und dazu, sich die Straße zurück zu nehmen, unabhängig davon, was die Polizei und der Staat dazu sagen. Denn unseren „Schutz gewährleisten“ können sie nie, auch wenn sie gerade mal nicht selber die anti-queere Gewalt ausüben.

Unsere Lebensweisen als queere, als migrantische, als trans, als behinderte Menschen und als Frauen werden immer wieder angegriffen durch gewalttätige patriarchale, autoritäre und faschistische Personen, Gruppierungen und Strukturen, wie z.B. auch die AfD. In diesem Sinne rufen wir dazu auf, uns zu organisieren und diesen Angriffen entschlossen, mit gegenseitiger Fürsorge und Solidarität und auch der notwendigen Militanz entgegenzutreten.
Wir stellen uns klar gegen die rassistische und anti-muslimische Instrumentalisierung der Tat.
Wir schicken allen Betroffenen, Trauernden und Kämpfenden Kraft und den Mut zum Widerstand.
Mehr queere Riots! Remember Stonewall!
Liebevolle und solidarische Grüße aus dem LesBiSchwulTransQueeren* Tortenessen, Bern
Courage for collective queer self defense!

content:
Auteur·e

: Le Révolté

Titre

: Les Préludes de la Révolution

Date

: 1882

Notes

: Premier article du 

Révolté

 du 28 octobre 1882, réagissant aux troubles de Montceau-les-Mines, à la mise en mouvement de la Bande noire et à leur premier procès. L'auteur·e est peut-être Jean Grave, mais ce n'est pas certain.

Source

: Extrait le 16 juillet 2026 de <

fr.wikisource.org/wiki/Les_Pr%C3%A9ludes_de_la_R%C3%A9volution

>.




 Nous sommes en pleine insurrection en France. Chaque jour le télégraphe nous apprend de nouvelles tentatives dirigées contre les patrons, la prêtraille, les agents du gouvernement. On arrête des mineurs qui sortent des puits avec de la dynamite et de la poudre dans les poches. Les attaques contre les patrons ou leurs sicaires ; les lettres menaçantes, les affiches révolutionnaires surgissent de tous côtés. Paris se met de la partie et appelle à la vengeance contre les propriétaires de maisons ; les murs de Marseille, du Creusot se couvrent de placards. Le mouvement tend à s’étendre. L’ouvrier, courbé depuis des siècles sous le joug des exploiteurs, redresse la tête en apprenant que ses frères s’insurgent ; et le bourgeois sent le frisson au dos en voyant le caractère nouveau que prend cette fois-ci le mouvement populaire. 




 En effet, il n’y a plus à en douter, nous sommes en présence d’un de ces mouvements qui sont les préludes de la Révolution. C’est un des précurseurs de la Jacquerie du dix-neuvième siècle : non pas d’une Jacquerie dirigée, comme au siècle passé, contre les seigneurs — il fut facile à la bourgeoisie de maîtriser celle-ci et de l’utiliser à son profit, — mais de cette Jacquerie que craignaient tant les Robespierre et les Conventionnels, dirigée contre tous les détenteurs de la richesse sociale : des usines, des manufactures, des mines, des maisons, de la banque etc., et contre leurs supports naturels : le prêtre, le gendarme, le juge, le fonctionnaire, le gouvernant, quel que soit le nom qu’il se donne. Toutes les révolutions vraiment populaires ont commencé de même : par des actes isolés, comme ceux de Florian et de Fournier, et par des émeutes partielles, comme celles de Montceau et de Blanzy. Les paysans d’avant 1789 n’ont pas fait autrement, lorsqu’ils faisaient, pendant treize ans, la petite guerre aux seigneurs et à leurs agents, en attendant le moment où il devint possible de promener la torche sur les châteaux pour abolir les derniers vestiges du servage. 




 Ce qui distingue le mouvement du bassin de Blanzy, de tous les mouvements que nous avons vu se produire en France depuis plus de trente ans, et ce qui lui donne surtout l’importance qu’il a acquise pour la prochaine révolution, — c’est le choix de l’ennemi, c’est la manière dont il porte ses coups, c’est son indépendance de toute clique de politiqueurs bourgeois. L’impulsion révolutionnaire n’a jamais manqué au peuple français ; mais depuis trente ans on a toujours vu les travailleurs suivre les meneurs de la bourgeoisie. Le peuple accourait en masse aux manifestations, mais lui-même n’en était pas l’instigateur : il endossait un programme qui n’était pas le sien. Il suivait les comités de politiciens, et réclamait ce que la bourgeoisie tenait à réclamer à un moment donné. Demandait-elle, par exemple, la réforme du système électoral, le travailleur criait « la Réforme ! » et se laissait berner par ce raisonnement : — « Obtenons d’abord la réforme, ou bien la république ; alors, le gouvernement porté par nous au pouvoir, fondé sur nos épaules, sera obligé de s’occuper de nos réclamations. Le refuserait-il, ne sommes-nous pas là pour lui forcer la main au besoin ? » — Et les travailleurs manifestaient, dressaient des barricades, opposaient leurs poitrines aux baïonnettes de la troupe et finissaient par tomber un gouvernement. On sait le reste. Les nouveaux venus faisaient ripaille à leur tour, s’empressaient de se caser, eux et les leurs, jouaient au fonctionnarisme, et lorsque le peuple rappelait les belles promesses de la veille, le nouveau gouvernement était assez fort pour mitrailler les mécontents. 




 Cette fois-ci, les choses se passent autrement. Ce n’est plus pour le compte de la bourgeoisie que s’insurgent les mineurs. Ce n’est plus dans les conciliabules des politiqueurs qu’ils vont chercher le mot d’ordre ; ce n’est plus aux bourgeois, ni aux ouvriers embourgeoisés, qu’ils vont s’adresser pour qu’on les organise et les mène à la baguette. Ils marchent eux-mêmes et suivent leur voie. C’est pour mettre fin à l’exploitation odieuse dont ils sont las et humiliés, qu’ils s’arment de dynamite et de revolvers. Ils ne se laissent plus berner par ce sophisme qui consiste à dire que pour se défaire du patron exploiteur, il faut changer de maître : ils vont droit au patron. Et si, comme dans tous les mouvements populaires, les premiers coups se dirigent vers le côté de la plus faible résistance, là où les initiateurs espèrent être mieux soutenus par les masses, encore inertes ; si l’on voit encore une certaine hésitation lorsqu’il s’agit d’aborder le repaire de l’ours-exploiteur — hésitation très naturelle et fort bien connue par ceux qui savent ce que c’est qu’une émeute, — il n’en pas moins vrai que l’idée mère du soulèvement s’exprime par ces cris qui retentissent sous les plis du drapeau rouge : « 

Vive la Révolution Sociale ! Vive 93 ! Vive l’Anarchie ! Mort aux bourgeois !

 » 




 Ce cri ne périra pas. Affirmé par l’émeute, il se retrouvera le jour du grand soulèvement.
